title: M51, the Whirlpool Nebula, NGC 5194/5195.
caption: The Whirlpool Galaxy, M51 (NGC 5194/5195), imaged by the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
celestial: M51, NGC 5194, NGC 5195, Whirlpool Galaxy · constellation Canes Venatici

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This colour view shows M51, the Whirlpool, made up of the large spiral galaxy NGC 5194 and its smaller, barred and more shapeless companion NGC 5195. The companion takes on a reddish tint because it sits behind the dusty arm that links it to the main galaxy.

M51 has a place in the history of astronomy. In 1845 the Third Earl of Rosse made out spiral structure here, the first time it had been seen in any astronomical object. Its arms are perhaps the neatest textbook example in any nearby galaxy, and such regularity suggests something keeps them in shape. The tidal pull of NGC 5195 may do it, by generating spiral density waves.

Although the Whirlpool is smaller and less massive than our own Galaxy, it is considerably brighter. That is because recent star formation has filled it with hot, luminous young stars of the O and B types.
scale: M51 lies approximately 31 million light-years away and is over 65,000 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Three CCD frames from the Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope, taken through filters roughly matching red, green and blue, were combined to recreate a true-colour picture. The colour balance was reworked in July 2000.
understand.eye: The combined CCD exposures gather far more light than the eye can, bringing out colour and detail in the galaxies.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Because the system is so large on the sky, the image was made with a 'drift scan', in which the telescope stayed fixed while the sky moved across the detector, with each row of the chip shifted along in step. The same spiral pattern also shows up in radio emission, suggesting the galaxy's magnetic fields are squeezed by the density wave.
alt: A spiral galaxy with well-defined arms, one of which connects to a smaller, reddish companion galaxy.
